claims.text: High-throughput first-principles calculations combined with machine-learning potential development can accurately determine melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys.
The proposed approach can determine these properties efficiently.
High-throughput first-principles calculations can be used to develop a machine-learning-based potential for high-entropy alloys.
First-principles calculations or molecular-dynamics simulations provide the mechanism for predicting the stated thermodynamic properties.
Melting temperatures can be predicted within 10 K of experimental values.
Enthalpies of fusion can be predicted within 5% of experimental values.
Entropies of fusion can be predicted within 5% of experimental values.
Volume changes at melting can be predicted within 2% of experimental values.
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties can be predicted within 5% of experimental values.
The approach applies to high-entropy alloys containing three to six principal elements.
The approach applies at temperatures up to 2000 K.
Machine-learning potential development introduces uncertainty into the predictions.
Experimental data available for validation are limited.
The approach can be tested by comparing predicted and experimental thermodynamic properties for a set of high-entropy alloys.
Deviation greater than 20% from experiment for any measured property is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed performance targets are much stricter than the 20% falsification threshold. Predictions could substantially fail every stated accuracy target—for example, exceeding 10 K error in melting temperature or 2% error in volume change—without falsifying the hypothesis under the stated rule.
